controversies/prosperity-and-new-apostle: Does faith guarantee health and wealth, and are there apostles and prophets today?
Prosperity gospel and the New Apostolic Reformation

Since the 1970s, two influential streams within independent charismatic Christianity, the Word of Faith/prosperity gospel and the New Apostolic Reformation, have provoked strong criticism from evangelicals, Pentecostal denominations and Catholic bishops, while flourishing in the Global South and in American media.

Christ became poor that we might become rich, and by his stripes we were healed. God is not glorified by his children living in sickness and lack. When believers speak God’s promises in faith and sow generously, they reap the blessing the covenant guarantees, and that message is good news to the world’s poor.
Suffering and contentment in the New Testament

Christ gave apostles and prophets as well as pastors and teachers until the Church reaches maturity. God is again raising apostolic leaders to equip the saints and prophets to give direction, so that the Church can disciple whole nations and every sphere of society.

The Spirit’s gifts are real, but the gospel is the message of the cross, not a technique for wealth, and the apostles’ foundational authority is not transferable. The Lausanne Movement, Pentecostal scholars and many African theologians warn that these movements exploit the poor, silence accountability and confuse the kingdom of God with worldly success or political power.
Love of money is a root of evil (1 Tim 6:10)

controversies/original-guilt-east-and-we: Do all humans inherit Adam’s guilt, or only the death and corruption his sin unleashed?
Original sin: inherited guilt or ancestral corruption?

Western churches since Augustine have taught that Adam’s descendants inherit guilt as well as corruption; the Greek, Syriac and Coptic traditions speak of inherited mortality and a wounded nature, and in the 20th century Orthodox theologians sharpened this into a critique of Augustine. Zwingli and later Arminians offered a Western middle way.

Paul says that through one man’s disobedience many were made sinners and that judgement came upon all to condemnation. Infants are baptised for the remission of sins. Humanity is one in Adam as believers are one in Christ; if we cannot be condemned in Adam we cannot be justified in Christ. Experience confirms that sin is not learned by imitation alone but is rooted in our nature.
Ezekiel 18:20: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father
Reliance on the Latin in quo of Romans 5:12

Guilt is personal; what Adam bequeathed was death. Because we are mortal and fear death, we grasp at self-preservation and sin. Christ, trampling down death by death, heals our nature and frees us from the devil’s tyranny. To speak of infants as guilty misunderstands both justice and baptism, which is illumination and new life.
Paschal theology of victory over death
Later Orthodox confessions used inherited-sin language

Original sin is real and deadly, a disease inclining every human to self-love, but it is not personal guilt until it issues in actual sin. This view preserves divine justice toward infants while affirming the universality of sin and the need for Christ.
Condemned in the Augsburg Confession for minimising sin

Westminster Confession teaches imputation of Adam’s guilt.

Unresolved and largely unaddressed in formal dialogue. Catholic teaching (Catechism 404-405) says original sin is “contracted” not “committed”, a sin only in an analogical sense, which narrows the gap with the East; Reformed federalism and Orthodox ancestral-sin teaching remain far apart. Questions raised by evolutionary science have reopened the debate in all traditions.

Underlies the contrast between forensic and therapeutic models of salvation.
Debates on human origins (historical Adam) have revived interest in Eastern and Irenaean alternatives.
controversies/image-of-god-and-human-hie: Does the image of God in every human being overturn hierarchies of race and sex — and why did Christians so often defend them?
The image of God, race and gender

Christian anthropology affirms that all humans bear God’s image, yet for centuries theologians also justified the subordination of women, the conquest of Indigenous peoples and racial slavery. Debates at Valladolid (1550), over American slavery and apartheid, and in feminist, Black and womanist theologies turned on how the image of God and the doctrine of sin apply to these hierarchies.
Hierarchical readings (historic)

Advocates claimed that God ordered creation hierarchically: Aristotle’s philosophy and texts such as Genesis 3:16, 9:25-27 and the household codes seemed to show natural ranks among peoples and between men and women. Order, they argued, was itself a good of creation, and subordination need not deny spiritual equality before God (Galatians 3:28 was read as concerning salvation, not society).

Every human being, of every people and both sexes, is made in God’s image and redeemed by Christ. Las Casas insisted that the peoples of the Americas were rational image-bearers to be won by persuasion, not the sword; abolitionists and later Black, feminist and womanist theologians argued that racism and sexism are themselves sin, and that the doctrine of sin has often been written from the standpoint of the powerful.

controversies/legal-vs-union-gospel-deba: Is the gospel fundamentally God’s legal verdict of acquittal for those who believe, or the announcement of humanity’s inclusion and adoption in the incarnate Son?
Legal gospel vs gospel of union

A debate running from McLeod Campbell’s deposition (1831) through Barth and the Torrances’ critique of federal Calvinism to contemporary controversies over Trinitarian "inclusion" theology, the Mirror Bible and the global grace message.
Legal / forensic framework

The gospel is good news because the bad news is real: we stand guilty before a holy God. In Christ, God himself has kept the law and borne its curse for us, and through faith alone we receive a verdict that will never be reversed. Union with Christ is precious, but without imputed righteousness and propitiation, "union" becomes a vague sentiment and assurance has no foundation.
Paul’s forensic vocabulary.

Relational / union framework

The gospel begins with the Father, Son and Spirit, not with a law above God. The Son became what we are so that we might share what he is; he gathered all humanity into his life, death and resurrection. Faith does not make this true; it is the Spirit opening our eyes to it. Only so is assurance Christ-centred and the gospel truly good news for all.
